Reports from staff and volunteers highlight notable improvements in children's growth, physical strength, confidence, and social interaction, attributed to play therapy and supplementary feeding programs. Despite the implementation of a close and continuous care model, not all children were tested for HIV. Among those attending play centers, 59% underwent HIV testing. Testing for HIV required the consent of a caregiver or guardian and was only pursued if it was deemed in the best interest of the child. This best interest was defined as ensuring the child would benefit from treatment without facing stigma, discrimination, or isolation. All children diagnosed as HIV-positive successfully transitioned from diagnosis to treatment. The use of standardized registers proved effective in preventing loss to follow-up. Guardians of children who missed their medications were visited at home and provided with support and assistance by community mobilizers. In Rwanda, Heineken Breweries, in partnership with PharmAccess International Foundation, launched the Heineken Access to HAART Programme in 2001 to address HIV/AIDS among its employees. This program, part of a comprehensive HIV prevention strategy, was later expanded to all Heineken African Operating Companies, as well as Vietnam and Cambodia. The program offers benefits to employees and their immediate dependents, including children, as an addition to existing medical care services. Once enrolled in HIV treatment, patients retain access to care for life, even if they are laid off. By January 2005, 736 out of 2,595 eligible individuals in Rwanda had received HIV testing services (HTS), identifying 109 HIV-positive individuals (15%). The program has grown in participation as employees observed successful treatment outcomes and Heineken's commitment to non-discrimination. In Uganda, modern quality improvement approaches have been adopted to enhance linkage and enrollment from HTS into care and treatment. Interventions such as providing peer escorts to ART clinics and enrolling HIV-positive clients into care on the same day significantly improved linkage rates, increasing from 58% in August 2013 to 89% in April 2014. Reproductive Health Uganda (RHU) implemented a three-year project in Kampala's urban slums to improve access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and HIV services for sex workers. Peer-led, community-based programs provided comprehensive SRH and HIV services, including mobile and home-based HTS. Over 1,000 sex workers received HTS, and 350 individuals were newly diagnosed as HIV-positive, with most linked to care and treatment. In Ghana, the SHARPER project addressed barriers to HTS for men who have sex with men (MSM) by engaging community liaison officers (CLOs) to conduct outreach through social media and mobile HTS services. Between December 2012 and March 2014, seven mobile HTS sessions were conducted, with 56% of participants accepting testing. Among those tested, 25 were diagnosed as HIV-positive and enrolled in care. The program's success relied on building trust and collaboration between stakeholders and key populations. In Namibia, the Strengthening HIV Prevention, Care, and Treatment among Key Populations project began in 2011, focusing on MSM, sex workers, and their clients. Services included mobile and moonlight HTS facilities, risk reduction counseling, and linkage to ART. Between October 2013 and September 2014, 12,609 sex workers and 2,219 MSM received HIV prevention interventions, with 236 clients diagnosed as HIV-positive and initiated on ART. In South Africa, the Voices of Change program, launched in 2011, provided mobile clinical services to sex workers in high HIV transmission areas. From 2011 to 2015, 12,993 HIV tests were conducted, with a positivity rate of 13%. The program emphasized user-friendly, stigma-free services and achieved high client satisfaction rates. In Bolivia, the Association Ibis-Hivos developed a mobile health service strategy to reach MSM and transgender individuals with HTS and risk-reduction services. Over two years, 6,541 rapid tests were performed, identifying 51 confirmed HIV-positive cases. The strategy effectively addressed barriers to healthcare access. In Lebanon, the Marsa medical center, established in 2011, provides sexual health services to key populations, including MSM, sex workers, and transgender individuals. The center offers HTS, general medical consultations, and psychosocial counseling. Between 2011 and 2015, Marsa conducted over 4,000 HIV tests, diagnosing 69 MSM as HIV-positive. The program's success is supported by the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health and the National AIDS Control Programme. In Pakistan, the Nai Zindagi Foundation focuses on empowering people who inject drugs and their partners through HTS and other services. From 2012 to 2013, 11,430 individuals accepted HTS, with 2,839 testing HIV-positive. Regular retesting is recommended due to the high risk of HIV transmission through unsafe injections. In Brazil, the Viva Melhor Sabendo project, launched in 2014, aims to increase HIV testing among key populations, including MSM, transgender individuals, and sex workers. Peer educators provide oral-fluid-based rapid HIV testing in accessible venues. From May 2014 to March 2015, 28,400 tests were conducted, with 82% of HIV-positive individuals referred for confirmatory testing and care. In Morocco, the Association de Lutte Contre le Sida (ALCS) has been providing HTS since 1992. Advocacy efforts led to policy changes, enabling immediate post-test counseling and referral to HIV Care Units. Between 2011 and 2015, ALCS provided over 4,000 HIV tests, with strong support from the National AIDS Program. These programs demonstrate the importance of tailored, community-based approaches to improve access to HIV testing, care, and treatment, particularly among key populations facing stigma and discrimination.
